passage_changes.passage: The Indian rupee depreciated by over 5% in 2025 and, by December, had crossed 90 per US dollar. The fall was not the result of one sudden shock. Analysts instead pointed to a mix of global and domestic pressures that had been building over time. Strength in the US dollar was a major backdrop, and the rupee was also hit by delays in a trade arrangement between India and the United States that investors had been anticipating. Money flowed out of Indian markets as global risk sentiment shifted. On the domestic side, the gap between what India buys from abroad and what it sells drew close attention. Crude oil prices rose, and some exports to major destinations were under strain. Demand for dollars also grew in the currency market as businesses and traders responded to the expectation of further weakness in the rupee. The 90 level drew particular attention from traders, who treat such round-number thresholds as important. Market participants said the fall had built up over time rather than arriving in a single day. Experts said the rupee's path in the months ahead would depend on global financial conditions, external trade developments and domestic economic indicators.

The Durand Line is a long international boundary that separates Pakistan from Afghanistan. Its origins lie in the colonial period, when British India and Afghanistan were locked in a long and often violent relationship. Britain fought several wars with Afghanistan, and some of these conflicts ended in settlements that changed how Afghanistan's external relations were handled. The boundary itself was fixed through a late nineteenth-century arrangement that involved British officials and the Afghan ruler of the time. Its path crosses demanding terrain, from mountain ranges in the north to deserts further south. When British rule over the subcontinent ended, the boundary passed to Pakistan, while Afghanistan has continued to question its legitimacy. Many communities that live near the line share ethnic and cultural ties across it, so the boundary affects families and tribes as well as governments. Tensions along the frontier have periodically resurfaced, and recent allegations of airstrikes near the line have drawn fresh attention to a dispute that began more than a century ago. Students preparing for current affairs should understand both the historical background and the modern implications of this boundary, since disputes of this kind shape regional security and diplomacy. Diplomatic exchanges about the border have often focused on whether the boundary is legitimate, and these debates continue to shape relations between the neighbouring states.

Restoring degraded land has become a central goal in the Aravalli region, where mining and urban growth have put pressure on the landscape for decades. Planners have drawn inspiration from a large African project that aims to hold back the spread of desert. The approach focuses on planting native species on degraded land to support ongoing afforestation. Nurseries are set up to grow saplings for continuing planting drives, so that seedlings are ready when they are needed. Damaged water bodies are also being restored, because healthy ponds and lakes help recharge groundwater. Invasive plant species, which crowd out native plants, are removed so that the native forest can recover. The work is coordinated centrally but depends on many partners, including non-governmental organisations, private companies and local communities. The National Forest Policy (1988) aims for at least one-third of total land area under forest or tree cover. The restoration is meant to control desertification, improve air quality and strengthen climate resilience in the Delhi-NCR region. Together, these measures aim to protect the region's green cover and water supply. The nurseries and planting drives span the states that the corridor crosses, including Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi. Plantation work covers degraded land, and the approach relies on species that grow naturally in the region.

A Uniform Civil Code would mean one common set of personal laws that applies to all citizens, irrespective of their religious affiliation. The framers of the Constitution did not intend total uniformity in this area. The Central Government favours a common code, calling different matrimonial laws for various religions a threat to the nation's unity. The 2018 Law Commission report suggested reforming and codifying family laws across religions instead of pursuing a UCC at this stage. The Supreme Court has also referred to the matter in several judgments. In the Shah Bano case, the Court highlighted the need for uniformity in personal laws. Later rulings on talaq-e-biddat, also called triple talaq, dealt with a practice within personal law. The Court has also praised one Indian state that has a functioning UCC, calling it an example for others. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 also contains an offence for marrying again during the lifetime of a spouse, which is punishable with imprisonment and a fine. Personal laws continue to differ across religions in matters of marriage and property, and this difference is the core of the debate. Together these strands show how the UCC debate connects constitutional text, legislative reform and judicial rulings.

When the rupee faces sustained pressure, policymakers can work on several fronts at once. One approach is to reduce how much India's trade depends on the dollar, so that more transactions with partner countries are settled in the domestic currency. A second approach is to make the rupee easier to trade and hold outside India, which would widen its use in global markets. Strengthening the external sector is another route, and this includes maintaining healthy foreign exchange reserves. The central bank can also step into the currency market, selling or buying dollars as conditions require, and it can adjust interest rates. Over the longer term, attention turns to structural matters. Improving export competitiveness, attracting foreign direct investment through better infrastructure and regulation, and making it easier to do business are all part of this picture. Gold imports also weigh on the external balance, so reducing them is part of the broader effort. Policy choices are also shaped by the need to control inflation. Taken together, these steps aim to ease pressure on the currency gradually, rather than resolving it in a single move.

Economic news in December 2025 focused on how stable the Indian economy looked and how the banking system is being watched more closely. The Reserve Bank of India, which decides monetary policy, recently reduced its key policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point. The central bank described the situation as a rare Goldilocks phase, a term that describes an economy in a balanced state. In such a phase, growth is steady, inflation is low, employment is high and the economy shows no sign of overheating or recession. Regulators have also taken steps to strengthen the largest banks. Some banks are so large and so closely connected with the rest of the system that their failure could disrupt the entire economy, so they must hold extra capital. For customers, the RBI's grievance system has been reorganised. A single integrated scheme now handles complaints against banks, non-banking finance companies and other regulated entities, with the aim of resolving disputes quickly, transparently and at low cost. Looking ahead, the government will conduct another Economic Census once the population census is complete, with the data expected to support a unified business register and better planning for enterprises across the country. Together, these measures show how monetary policy, banking regulation, consumer protection and statistics work as connected parts of the financial system.

facts.title: International Relations and Trade
facts.summary: This group covers the Durand Line, the 2,600 km boundary between Pakistan and Afghanistan that was fixed by a British-era agreement and has been contested since Partition. It also covers India's trade agreements with New Zealand and Oman expand trade and investment, with zero-duty access stated only for New Zealand. The section closes with the US National Security Strategy, the Preah Vihear temple dispute, and India's re-election to the IMO Council.
facts: The Durand Line is a 2,600 km international boundary between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
It was drawn through the Durand Agreement of 1893 between Sir Henry Mortimer Durand and Emir Abdur Rahman Khan.
Afghanistan refused to formally recognise the Durand Line, viewing it as a colonial imposition.
Treaty of Gandamak (1879) granted Britain control over Afghanistan's foreign affairs.
Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919) restored Afghanistan's foreign policy autonomy while reaffirming the Durand Line.
India-New Zealand FTA gives 100% of Indian exports to New Zealand zero-duty market access.
India-Oman CEPA is India's second CEPA in the GCC after the UAE and aims to expand trade beyond USD 10 billion.
US National Security Strategy reasserts the Monroe Doctrine (1823) and avoids branding Russia and China as existential threats.
ICJ (1962) gave sovereignty over Preah Vihear Temple to Cambodia; the 2013 ICJ clarification called for a demilitarised zone that was never fully implemented.
India was re-elected to the IMO Council's Category B for 2026-27 with the highest votes.
